pages.name: Lay it yourself
pages.task: Here the line sits above every reading. Drag its two handles to lay it through their middle, then press Check.
pages.why: A line through the middle leaves about as many readings above it as below, with short sticks spread along it. Four above, four below and no stick longer than 0.4 Ω will do. The dashed line, `_R_ = 0.04_T_ + 10`, is one that does.

pages.name: Read the law
pages.text: Take the law from the line, not the readings. Two points on it far apart, at 20 °C and 70 °C, rise 2.0 Ω over 50 °C, so the [[gradient]] is 0.04 Ω per °C. Carried back to 0 °C, the line gives `_c_ = 10.0 Ω`.

pages.name: Find the gradient
pages.task: What is the gradient of the line through the winding's readings?
pages.why: Two points on the line, far apart: 10.8 Ω at 20 °C and 12.8 Ω at 70 °C. The rise is `12.8 − 10.8 = 2.0 Ω` and the run `70 − 20 = 50 °C`, so the gradient is `2.0 Ω ÷ 50 °C = 0.04 Ω per °C`. The readings at 20 and 30 °C give `0.8 Ω ÷ 10 °C = 0.08 Ω per °C`, twice the line's, because each brings its own stray.

pages.name: R at 0 °C
pages.task: The line through the middle passes 10.8 Ω at 20 °C and climbs 0.04 Ω per °C. What does the winding read at 0 °C?
pages.why: Carry the line back 20 °C from 10.8 Ω at 20 °C. It falls `0.04 × 20 = 0.8 Ω`, so `_c_ = 10.8 − 0.8 = 10.0 Ω`, and the law is `_R_ = 0.04_T_ + 10`. That trusts the line to stay straight below the readings.

pages.name: Which two points?
pages.task: Each height is read off the line to within 0.1 Ω. Which two points give the most trustworthy gradient?
pages.why: Read each height to within 0.1 Ω. Between 20 and 70 °C the rise of 2.0 Ω could be 1.8 to 2.2 Ω, a gradient from 0.036 to 0.044 Ω per °C. Between 40 and 50 °C the rise of 0.4 Ω could be 0.2 to 0.6 Ω, anywhere from 0.02 to 0.06. The same slip is a small part of a big rise.

pages.text: With no force a spring does not stretch, so its line is pinned through (0, 0). Up to the [[limit of proportionality]], six example readings sit three above and three below `_F_ = 2.5_x_`. Past it the last two bend away below, so they are left out of the fit.

pages.name: Spring constant
pages.task: The same spring, its line fitted to the straight part. What is its spring constant?
pages.why: The line through the straight part is pinned at (0, 0) and passes 27.5 N at 11 mm. Rise ÷ run is `27.5 N ÷ 11 mm = 2.5 N per mm`, and that gradient is the [[spring constant]]. The last two readings, at 14 and 16 mm, are past the limit and left out.

pages.name: Read its law
pages.task: Line C passes 15 N at 60 N of load and 39 N at 220 N. What is its law?
pages.why: Read the line between the readings. The rise is `39 − 15 = 24 N` of effort over a run of `220 − 60 = 160 N` of load, so `_a_ = 24 ÷ 160 = 0.15`. Carry the line back to no load: `_b_ = 15 − 0.15 × 60 = 6 N`. So `_P_ = 0.15_W_ + 6`.
